title: Two Schools, Two Approaches
author: Mark Doggett
summary: Doggett, a retired engineering professor, uses the simultaneous opening of two new high schools in Bowling Green, Kentucky as a case study in competing answers to what secondary education is for. The Impact Center for Leadership and Innovation builds on career and technical education, industry certifications, and work based learning aimed at an emerging economy; Chesterton Academy offers classical liberal arts inside an explicitly Catholic framework organized around truth, goodness, and beauty. He grants each its strongest claim and then names its exposure. The career pathway delivers immediately usable skills but sits closest to the work AI automates, since precisely definable tasks are the first to go, and it must also carry the recurring cost of keeping specialized labs and equipment current. The classical model may age better because reasoning, communication, and judgment outlast particular technical knowledge, though it offers less for a student wanting advanced laboratory science or engineering, and its religious mission will not suit every family. His conclusion sidesteps the curricular contest entirely: the decisive variable is the culture each school builds, since no curriculum or technology substitutes for adults who hold high expectations. He ends by reframing the parental question from what children will learn to what kind of people they will become, and insists both schools should be held to both standards.
points: The comparison is concrete rather than abstract, set on two schools opening their inaugural year in the same small city with opposed philosophies.
Doggett argues the career and technical model is the more AI exposed of the two, because tasks that can be precisely defined and programmed automate first.
He makes the durability case for classical liberal education in economic terms, noting technical knowledge obsolesces while reasoning and judgment do not.
He is candid about the classical school's cost, listing fewer opportunities in advanced mathematics, laboratory science, engineering, and computer science.
The essay's pivot is that culture, not curriculum, is the most important difference between the two institutions.
quotes: School has started with much anticipation, and parents are increasingly concerned about the quality and purpose of their children’s education.

The Impact Center combines a traditional curriculum with specialized career and college pathways. It emphasizes career and technical education, industry certifications, leadership development, and project- and work-based learning.

Chesterton Academy, by contrast, provides a classical liberal-arts education within an explicitly Catholic intellectual and spiritual framework. Its educational goal is the pursuit of truth, goodness, and beauty, with faith integrated throughout the curriculum.

However, few skills are truly immune to artificial intelligence. Tasks that can be precisely defined and programmed are increasingly vulnerable to automation, making adaptability, problem-solving, communication, and leadership increasingly important.
Technical knowledge can become obsolete quickly, while the ability to reason, communicate, learn, adapt, and make sound judgments may prove more durable.

An uplifting learning environment requires excellent teachers, strong leadership, high expectations, and engaged parents. A school can have an impressive curriculum and sophisticated technology, but none can substitute for people who encourage students to work hard, take responsibility, and pursue excellence.
As a former public educator, I have learned that curriculum is only as good as the educational system and the people who deliver it.
In an age of artificial intelligence and rapid technological change, perhaps the most important question is not simply what our children will learn, but what kind of people they will become.
